subject: Quantitative Aptitude
topic: Permutation and Combination — Arrangements, Selections and Special Cases (W10)

questions.stem: In how many ways can 5 people be arranged in a row?
questions.explanation: C is correct. Number of arrangements = 5! = 5×4×3×2×1 = 120. This is a permutation problem where all 5 people are arranged in all 5 positions. Trap: 60 = 5!/2 (halved incorrectly); 100 = 5×5×4/... (wrong formula).

questions.stem: In how many ways can 3 students be selected from a group of 8?
questions.explanation: B is correct. C(8,3) = 8!/(3!×5!) = (8×7×6)/(3×2×1) = 336/6 = 56. This is a combination (order doesn't matter — we're selecting, not arranging). Trap: 336 = P(8,3) = 8×7×6 (permutation — order matters); 120 = C(10,3) (wrong total).

questions.stem: In how many ways can 3 books be selected from 7 different books and then arranged on a shelf?
questions.explanation: C is correct. First select 3 from 7: C(7,3)=35. Then arrange them on the shelf: 3!=6 ways. Total = 35×6 = 210. Equivalently, P(7,3) = 7×6×5 = 210 (permutation of 3 from 7). Trap: 35 = C(7,3) (only selection, ignoring arrangement); 420 = P(7,3)×2 (over-counts).

questions.stem: A committee of 4 men and 3 women is to be formed from a group of 8 men and 6 women. In how many ways can this be done?
questions.explanation: C is correct. Select 4 men from 8: C(8,4) = 70. Select 3 women from 6: C(6,3) = 20. Total = 70×20 = 1400. Trap: 700 = C(8,4)×C(6,2) (wrong number of women selected); 2800 = 1400×2 (double-counts).

questions.stem: How many 3-digit numbers can be formed using the digits 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 without repetition?
questions.explanation: C is correct. P(5,3) = 5×4×3 = 60. We choose 3 digits from 5 (without repetition) and arrange them — this is a permutation. Trap: 30 = 5×3×2 (wrong product); 120 = 5! (uses all 5 digits, not just 3); 45 = C(5,3)×3 (misapplies combination).

questions.stem: In how many ways can the letters of the word 'BOOK' be arranged?
questions.explanation: B is correct. BOOK has 4 letters with 'O' repeated twice. Arrangements = 4!/2! = 24/2 = 12. Trap: 24 = 4! (ignores the repeated O, over-counts by treating both O's as distinct); 6 = C(4,2) (only combinations, not arrangements).

questions.stem: 5 people sit around a circular table. How many distinct seating arrangements are possible?
questions.explanation: C is correct. Circular arrangements = (n−1)! = (5−1)! = 4! = 24. In circular arrangements, we fix one person to remove rotational equivalences, then arrange the remaining 4: 4! = 24 ways. Trap: 120 = 5! treats circular as linear; 10 = C(5,2) (wrong formula entirely).

questions.stem: In how many ways can all letters of 'MASTER' be arranged such that the arrangement begins with 'M'?
questions.explanation: C is correct. 'M' is fixed at position 1. The remaining 5 letters (A,S,T,E,R) can be arranged in 5! = 120 ways. Trap: 720 = 6! (arranges all 6 without fixing M); 60 = 5!/2 (wrong divisor — all letters in MASTER are unique, no repetition).

questions.stem: From a group of 5 men and 4 women, a committee of 5 is to be formed with at least 2 women. In how many ways can this be done?
questions.explanation: C is correct. 'At least 2 women' means exactly 2W+3M, or 3W+2M, or 4W+1M. C(4,2)×C(5,3) + C(4,3)×C(5,2) + C(4,4)×C(5,1) = 6×10 + 4×10 + 1×5 = 60+40+5 = 105. Trap: 126 = C(9,5) (total without restriction); 90 = only first two cases (forgets 4W+1M case).

questions.stem: In how many ways can 4 different balls be distributed into 3 different boxes such that no box is empty?
questions.explanation: B is correct. Total distributions of 4 balls into 3 boxes = 3⁴=81. Subtract cases where at least one box is empty using inclusion-exclusion: cases with at least 1 empty box = C(3,1)×2⁴ − C(3,2)×1⁴ = 3×16−3×1 = 45. Valid = 81−45 = 36. Equivalently: Stirling number S(4,3)=6 ways to partition × 3!=6 arrangements = 36. Trap: 81 = all distributions (ignores empty box condition); 24 = 4! (permutation, wrong approach).
